passages.v01:c01:p0023: “Well, we’ve been pondering it for a while—throughout the whole winter, actually,” Thirza replied. “Mrs. Alexander Tranter came up here one day prior to Christmas and mentioned her plan to obtain a young girl from the Marden asylum in the spring. We figured we would obtain a boy. Obed is advancing in age, as you know—he has reached sixty—and he lacks his former agility. His heart causes him significant trouble. Furthermore, you are aware of how extremely difficult securing hired labor has become. No one can ever be hired except those foolish, partially grown young French boys; and the moment you successfully train one to your routine and teach him something, he leaves abruptly for the States or the lobster canneries. Initially, Obed proposed acquiring a Home boy. However, I gave a firm ‘no’ to that idea. ‘They might be perfectly fine—I am not claiming otherwise—but I will not take any London street Arabs,’ I stated. ‘At minimum, provide me with someone native born. A risk will exist, regardless of whom we obtain. Nevertheless, my mind will be more at ease and my night’s sleep will be sounder if we obtain a born Canadian.’ Thus, we ultimately resolved to request that Mrs. Tranter select one for us when she traveled across to retrieve her young girl. Learning last week that she was departing, we dispatched word to her through Richard Tranter’s family at Delford to fetch us an intelligent, promising boy around ten or eleven years old. We concluded that age would be optimal—sufficiently old to assist with chores immediately and sufficiently young to be raised correctly. Our intention is to provide him with schooling and a comfortable home. Today we received a telegram from Mrs. Alexander Tranter—delivered from the station by the mail-man—announcing their arrival on the five-thirty train this evening. Therefore, Obed departed for Alder River to meet him. Mrs. Tranter intends to leave him there. Naturally, she continues onward to Pale Sands station herself.”

You never showed jealousy, or malice, as a few of them did. Poor Em White came by to visit me yesterday. Do you recall that Em and I were great friends for three years while attending school? And subsequently we fell out at the time of the school concert. Ever since, we have not uttered a word to one another. Was it not foolish? Any occurrence of that sort appears foolish at present. However, Em and I resolved the former dispute yesterday. She mentioned that she would have conversed years back, except she believed I would refuse to. And I refrained from ever conversing with her since I was convinced she would refuse to converse with me. Is it not peculiar the way folks misjudge one another, Nell?
